tagline: A village of shared work and useful inventions.
intro: From Canterbury Center, where Captain Jeremiah Clough once kept a timber fort and trading post for the Pennacook, the byway runs out to the Shaker village in the eastern part of town. Founded in 1792, it held some 300 people in 100 buildings by the middle of the nineteenth century.

The Shakers farmed, sold seeds and herbal medicines, and made pails and brooms. They took to new machinery too, from telephones in 1901 to a washing machine of their own that won a gold medal at the 1876 Centennial Exposition. The last of them, Sister Ethel Hudson, died in 1992. The sugar maples along Meetinghouse Lane and Shaker Road are theirs too.

moments.title: Canterbury
moments.text: Canterbury Center keeps its town hall, country store and gazebo, and the historical society's museum in the old one-room Center Schoolhouse.

moments.title: Canterbury Shaker Village
moments.text: The community's own powerhouse, built in 1910, first lit sixteen buildings; now fields, gardens and mill ponds surround the original and reconstructed buildings of the museum.
